full_text:
In 1930 CE, the frontiers of human understanding were transformed through the indomitable persistence of Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.

At the time, the reigning scientific establishment in the field of Theoretical Astrophysics was constrained by orthodox paradigms that could no longer account for emerging experimental anomalies. While many researchers looked past these discrepancies or dismissed them as instrument artifacts, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar recognized that the anomaly was itself a beacon pointing toward an undiscovered law of nature.

Working from primary documentation recorded in *The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs (Astrophysical Journal, 1931)* (Vol. 74, pp. 81–82; Nobel Prize in Physics (1983)), the breakthrough emerged through painstaking methodology. Every alternative hypothesis was systematically tested, isolated, and eliminated under rigorous controls.

A nineteen-year-old Indian student sailing from Madras to England combined relativity and quantum mechanics to calculate that dying stars exceeding 1.44 times the mass of the Sun cannot resist gravitational collapse, predicting black holes decades ahead of his time.

The discovery of The Chandrasekhar Limit for White Dwarf Stars (1.44 Solar Masses) did not merely answer a localized puzzle; it triggered a profound paradigm shift across Theoretical Astrophysics. Today, its principles form the bedrock of modern empirical science, reminding every student that progress is forged when courageous curiosity meets disciplined observation.
